rubric.result: The objective promises one query that answers which rung the epic stands at, reading only the spec on disk, GitHub's copy of it and the milestone's issues, and carrying what would be created when there is something to create. Every part is in the diff: `ReadEpicGroom#execute` asks `EpicSpecs#mostRecent` (spec on disk), `PublishedSpecs#holds` (GitHub's copy), `EpicIssues#listOf` (the milestone's issues) and nothing else, in that order, short-circuiting at the first rung that answers — null spec is NO_SPEC, `!spec.isFrozen()` is DRAFT, `!isPublished` is AWAITING_PUBLICATION, empty milestone is GROOMABLE, `holding.some(isPromotable)` is GROOMED and otherwise AUTHORISED. 'What would be created' is `EpicGroom#planned`, asked at the GROOMABLE branch only, and carried in `EpicGroomRead.plan`. Nothing is stored and nothing else is asked, which is the whole of what the sentence promises.

The TDD line names `it('a frozen spec whose committed copy is not on the default branch waits and asks github for nothing else')` with state `awaiting-publication` and the `EpicIssues` and `EpicGroom` doubles never asked. The test at line 242 of the new test file builds exactly that input (`Mother.frozen()` with a `PublishedSpecsDouble(false)`) and asserts `read.state` is `EpicGroomState.AWAITING_PUBLICATION` plus `flow.issues.asked` and `flow.groom.asked` both `[]` — the same assertion, the same input, the same expected value. Its declared boundary pair is also there (line 257) and matches too: state `groomable`, `read.plan` is the very `GroomPlan` the groom double returned, and `flow.issues.asked` records `{ repository, milestone: Mother.TITLE }`, the spec's own title. The remaining four names from `**Tests:**` are present verbatim.

Compared name by name with the `Contract (backend/src/application/queries/read-epic-groom.ts)` block. `EpicGroomState` is a frozen object with the six members and the six literal values the block spells (`no-spec`, `draft`, `awaiting-publication`, `groomable`, `groomed`, `authorised`); `EpicGroomStateValue` is the same derived type; `ReadEpicGroomParams` takes `{ root: CheckoutRoot, repository: RepositoryName }`; `EpicGroomRead` declares the five readonly fields with the exact types given, including `readonly issues: readonly EpicIssue[]`; `ReadEpicGroom` takes `{ specs, published, issues, groom }` by name and `execute(params): Promise<EpicGroomRead>`. The block's prose is honoured too: the milestone is `EpicSpec#title()`, and `planned` is asked at one rung. No error and no new constant is prescribed, so nothing there to compare. On `spec.title()!`: the contract types the milestone as `string` while the port answers `string | null`, so the invariant had to be resolved somewhere; the diff resolves it the way the tree already does and I treat it under `patrones`.

Row by row against the diff. D-13 (no phase is stored) is the row this task is built on and the diff obeys it: the state is computed on every `execute` from the spec text, the published copy and the milestone's issues, and nothing is written anywhere. D-11 (a yardstick is imported, never reimplemented) holds: the freeze is read through `EpicSpec#isFrozen()` and the dry run through the `EpicGroom` port over `ct-groom`; the query grows no second opinion. D-10 (everything new under `backend/` is TypeScript) holds — two `.ts` files. D-22 and D-6 (the gates are the human's, refused with an explicit code) are untouched: this is a read with no act and no key, which is what the plan asks of task 4. D-25, D-18, D-21, D-1, D-7, D-23 and D-14 have no bearing on a derivation query and the diff implements nothing against them. No row is reopened.

Exemplars: `backend/src/application/queries/read-spec-freeze.ts` and `backend/__tests__/application/read-spec-freeze.test.ts` are the pair this diff plays the same role as, and the idiom matches line for line — a frozen `Params`, a frozen vocabulary, a frozen `Read` result object, ports injected by name, and a test with `*Double` subclasses of the real ports recording `asked`, a `Mother` of named scenarios and a `Flow` with `static readingSpec` and `run()`. ct's yardstick, document by document. `architecture.md`: the query lives in `application/queries` (the folder is the discriminator), imports only `domain/...` with `import type`, depends on ports and never on an adapter, has no suffix on the type, and declares its parameters object and its result object beside it — the shape that document prescribes for a use case. `style.md`: no comment or docstring in either file, English throughout, and no free function at module level — every function hangs off `ReadEpicGroom`, the doubles, `Mother` or `Flow`; the Spanish inside the fixture spec text (`**Estado:** CONGELADA`, `**Fecha de congelación:**`) is contract data that `CLAUDE.md` pins as parsed headings, so the English rule does not reach it. `decisions.md`: the milestone-name rule is decided once here and travels to the plugin as `--milestone` in `ct-groom-epic.ts`, and the promotable rule stays the single `EpicIssue#isPromotable()`; the state vocabulary exists in exactly one file (grep for `groomable`/`awaiting-publication` finds only this module and its test). `domain.md`: no tool noun enters the query. `boundaries.md`: no edge is crossed here — the ports are already the seam. `testing.md`: outside-in at the application layer with every port doubled at construction, values (`EpicSpec`, `EpicIssue`, `GroomPlan`) real and never doubled, the arrange built with mothers rather than with the piece under test, and the report declares the assertions it broke by hand (the awaiting-publication short circuit and the groomed/authorised branch) and restored. `simplicity.md`: `EpicGroomRead.spec` has no consumer in the tree today — the callers are tasks 5 and 6 of this same slice, and the field is spelled in the `Contract` block this task must state verbatim, so the burden the document asks for is discharged by the plan and not by the implementer; I record it here rather than as a finding, since a diff that dropped the field would fail `contrato`. On `spec.title()!` at line 88: `simplicity.md` says the guard lives where the value enters from outside and that a second opinion downstream 'defends against a caller that does not exist' — `DiskEpicSpecs#mostRecent` already throws `EpicSpecNotUnderstood` for a titleless spec — and `freeze-spec.ts:87` (`spec.frozenOn()!`) is the tree's own precedent for the same move. Neither yardstick has a sentence banning it in the application layer, so it is not a finding; the residual risk the implementer declared (a future adapter surfacing as a TypeError instead of a domain error) is real but belongs to the port's type, which this task's `**Files:**` does not open. `defects.md`, its four rules answered one by one. Closed vocabulary: complied — the classification is `EpicGroomState`, a frozen six-member vocabulary with a derived type, never a loose string or a boolean, and there is no dispatch over it in this diff and so no catch-all branch. Raw map as the return value of logic: complied — logic returns `EpicGroomRead`, a frozen value object; the named-object arguments handed to `holds`, `listOf` and `planned` are the ports' already-declared parameter bags, and no module in this diff receives a map and decides with it. Two fields that have to agree: complied — `state` carries information the other fields cannot reconstruct (NO_SPEC against DRAFT, GROOMED against AUTHORISED), so it is not a flag repeating another field's non-emptiness, and absence is carried by `null` in the type, never by an empty string or a zero. An error named for where it happens: no subject — this diff declares and raises no error.
The diff has no `-` lines at all: `364 insertions(+)`, both files new (`new file mode 100644`). There is no pre-existing test in it to remove, relax or rewrite, so this item has no subject.

The promised behaviour is produced by production code. `read-epic-groom.ts` holds every decision the objective names: the null-spec return, the `!spec.isFrozen()` return, the `!isPublished` return, the `holding.length === 0` branch that asks the dry run, and the `holding.some((issue) => issue.isPromotable())` ternary. The test's scaffolding (`EpicSpecsDouble`, `PublishedSpecsDouble`, `EpicIssuesDouble`, `EpicGroomDouble`, `Mother`, `Flow`) only supplies inputs and records what each port was asked; no expected state is hard-coded anywhere but in the production ladder. Revert `read-epic-groom.ts` and every one of the six tests stops passing — there is no state the doubles could produce on their own.

`**Files:**` declares the two new files and the diff writes those two and nothing else. Inside them, every line traces to a sentence: the six states, the params and result objects and the constructor come from the `Contract` block; the ladder order and the single dry run come from the task's own paragraph; the six tests are the six names `**TDD:**` and `**Tests:**` list, and `Mother.closedBacklogIssue()` exists only to make the AUTHORISED case the plan asked for. Nothing under `### Out of scope` is touched — no plugin script, no `--reconcile`, no dispatcher, no merge, no pull-request write, no repository column. There is no hunk of the plan file in this diff, so no amendment to rule on, and `docs/superpowers/metrics/issue-330.jsonl` shows as modified in the tree but is not staged and is not in this package.

Six new tests, all in `read-epic-groom.test.ts`, measured against the three properties. Deterministic: no clock, no network, no filesystem, no randomness and no sleep — the only date in the file is the literal `2026-09-14` inside `Mother.frozen()`'s text, which is data the assertion never reads. Isolated: each test constructs its own `Flow` with its own doubles, the only shared state is `Mother`'s statics and every one of them is frozen (`GroomPlan` and `GroomPlanIssue` call `Object.freeze` on themselves and their arrays), so nothing is left behind for the next test and no test depends on file order. Verifies real behaviour: the assertions are on what the query returned (`read.state`, `read.plan`, `read.issues`) and on what each port received (`flow.issues.asked`, `flow.groom.asked`), which `conventions/testing.md` names as the observable effect — none of them would survive reverting the production lines. I loaded `control-tower-loop:test-driven-development` and its `testing-anti-patterns.md` to measure the finer half: anti-pattern 1 (asserting on a mock's existence) does not bite, because the `asked` arrays assert which call production made and with which arguments rather than that the double is present; there is no test-only method on a production class; the doubles preserve the behaviour under test rather than removing a side effect the test needs; and mock setup is shorter than the assertions. The one thing I weighed and did not file: the first test's name carries an 'and' the skill's table would split, but the plan dictated that sentence literally in `**TDD:**` and splitting it would break `asercion-tdd`, so it is the plan's call and not the implementer's.
